title: Development of Ultrafast Four-dimensional Precession Electron Diffraction
content: Ultrafast transmission electron microscopy (UTEM) [1] is a combination of TEM and a femtosecond pulsed laser, which enables the investigation of ultrafast dynamics within photoexcited materials. Among the various applications, ultrafast electron diffraction (UED) [2] has played a crucial role in studying photoexcited crystal structure dynamics. UED has provided insights into various ultrafast phenomena, such as photoacoustic generation [3] and photoinduced structural phase transition [4]. One of the ultimate goals of UED is to quantitatively track the transient atomic positions. However, quantitative analysis based on the diffraction intensity is still challenging. The peak intensities of electron diffraction from single crystals are extremely sensitive to inhomogeneity inherent in TEM samples such as local rotation and strain. In addition, the strong multiple scattering inevitable in thick samples has prevented us from performing quantitative structural analysis. In static (equilibrium) cases, extensive efforts have been made to overcome this challenge. Precession electron diffraction (PED) is one of the successful methods to suppress the effect of sample inhomogeneities and multiple scattering. Using PED measurements, structural refinement of various solid materials has been achieved over the past decades [5, 6]. Therefore, also in the context of UED, the integration of PED is highly demanded.
